flashcards.q: What distinguishes a distributed monolith from real microservices?
flashcards.a: Physical topology looks the same (multiple processes/repos) but the services aren't independently deployable, usually due to a shared database or un-versioned synchronous contracts forcing coordinated deploys.
Writing to two systems (e.g. DB and queue) as two non-atomic operations; a crash or failure between them leaves the systems permanently disagreeing with no signal from either side.

flashcards.q: How does the transactional outbox pattern fix dual writes?
flashcards.a: Write the state change and an outbox event row in the same DB transaction; a separate relay (poller or CDC) publishes the event, retrying until acked â€” converts two unsafe writes into one atomic write plus a durable at-least-once relay.

flashcards.q: What guarantee does outbox/CDC actually provide, and what must consumers do?
flashcards.a: At-least-once delivery, not exactly-once. Consumers must be idempotent (dedupe by event ID) since the relay can republish after a failure between publish and ack.

flashcards.q: What is the highest-leverage single fix underlying most distributed-monolith and dual-write pain?
flashcards.a: Fixing shared-database ownership â€” giving each table exactly one writer/owning service, with other consumers going through an API or an event-derived read replica.

flashcards.q: What operational metrics reveal a god object?
flashcards.a: Disproportionate PR churn and merge-conflict rate concentrated in one file/class, and high bus-factor risk (few people understand the whole thing) â€” not size alone.

flashcards.q: Do the reliability and latency costs of chatty services scale the same way with call count?
flashcards.a: No. Latency compounds additively/multiplicatively along a sync chain (40 calls @10ms â‰ˆ 400ms floor); reliability compounds multiplicatively per-call success rate (99.9%^40 â‰ˆ 96% â€” a five-nines dependency set becomes a two-nines user experience).

flashcards.q: Name the three levers to fix chatty services.
flashcards.a: Aggregation (BFF fans out calls in parallel, cuts latency not count), data locality (local eventually-consistent replica via events, cuts call count), and reconsidering the boundary (merge always-called-together services).

flashcards.q: What is an anemic domain model and who named it?
flashcards.a: Entities that are pure data holders (getters/setters, no behavior) with all business logic in external *Service classes; named by Martin Fowler in 2003, reacting to J2EE-era entity beans.

flashcards.q: What's the overcorrection risk when fixing an anemic domain model?
flashcards.a: Stuffing the entity with responsibilities beyond its own invariants (external I/O, cross-entity orchestration) recreates the god-object problem inside what was meant to be a rich domain model.

flashcards.q: What's the scope line for what belongs on an entity vs. a service layer?
flashcards.a: If logic only needs the entity's own current fields, it belongs on the entity (order.can_cancel() checks self.status). If it needs another entity, external I/O, or multi-step orchestration, it belongs in a use-case/service layer.

flashcards.q: When is a shared database NOT the anti-pattern?
flashcards.a: When it's a deliberate, planned single-schema design for a small team needing real cross-entity ACID transactions, with one team owning the whole schema â€” the anti-pattern is specifically accidental, unplanned multi-writer coupling.

flashcards.q: When de-risking a 12-service distributed monolith, what's the actual unit you migrate â€” services or tables?
flashcards.a: Tables. Ownership, not the service diagram, is the real coupling graph; fix one table's ownership at a time (API or CDC replica cutover, reconciled in parallel, then old path removed) before revisiting whether the service boundaries themselves are wrong.

flashcards.q: What new failure mode does org-wide CDC (e.g. Debezium) introduce to fix dual writes?
flashcards.a: Every downstream consumer now implicitly depends on the source DB's WAL format and replication behavior â€” a schema change upstream can silently break every consumer at once, and replication lag creates new read-your-own-write bugs; the connector itself becomes a new operational single point of failure.

flashcards.q: Why is CDC still a net win over dual writes despite adding its own failure surface?
flashcards.a: Dual writes fail silently and randomly across many call sites (undetectable drift); CDC failures are visible (lag metrics, connector health, DLQ depth) and centralized in one place to monitor instead of N ad-hoc reconciliation jobs.
